extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; bankers and merchants interested in principles of banking and paper money
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of prudent banking practices and limits on paper-money issuance: reserve requirements, what banks should lend for, the hazards of over-issuance and of raising money by circulation (drawing-and-redrawing), and how banks should monitor customers' repayments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper money limited by underlying coin circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole paper money of every kind which can easily circulate in any country, never can exceed the value of the gold and silver, of which it supplies the place, or which ... would circulate there, if there was no paper money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith explains that if paper circulating exceeds what coin would otherwise circulate (given the lowest denomination of notes), the excess cannot be exported or used domestically and will return upon banks for conversion into coin, provoking runs. Example: if twenty-shilling notes are the lowest paper money current, total paper cannot exceed the gold/silver necessary for transactions of twenty shillings and upwards; any excess leads to immediate demand for payment from banks and an ensuing run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banks must keep larger reserves when circulation is excessive (and more than proportional)
rubrics_metrics.description: A banking company which issues more paper than can be employed in the circulation of the country ... ought to increase the quantity of gold and silver which they keep at all times in their coffers, not only in proportion to this excessive increase of their circulation, but in a much greater proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith gives a numeric illustration: if a bank's absorbable paper is £40,000 and it normally keeps £10,000 in coin, attempting to circulate £44,000 (an extra £4,000) will force it to hold not just £11,000 but £14,000 in coin. The excess circulation returns rapidly, so reserve requirements grow faster than issue; banks thus gain little from extra interest and suffer higher costs of collecting/replacing coin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-issuing paper money (do not exceed what circulation can absorb)
rubrics_metrics.description: A banking company which issues more paper than can be employed in the circulation of the country ... the excess could neither be sent abroad nor be employed in the circulation of the country, it must immediately return upon the banks, to be exchanged for gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-issuance provokes runs, forces banks to coin or buy bullion (sometimes at high prices), causes export of coin or melting into bullion, and increases operating costs (insurance, transport, agents). Historical examples: Bank of England's heavy annual coinage and Scotch banks' expense of employing agents in London; over-issue by projectors originally caused excessive circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only discount real bills payable when due (real-bills principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bank discounts to a merchant a real bill of exchange, drawn by a real creditor upon a real debtor, and which, as soon as it becomes due, is really paid by that debtor; it only advances to him a part of the value which he would otherwise be obliged to keep ... in ready money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such discounting advances only the portion of capital a merchant would otherwise keep idle; repayments replace the bank's advance when bills are paid, so the bank's coffers resemble a water-pond with inflows equal to outflows and requiring little extra expense to replenish. The safety of discounting depends on the bill being 'real' and promptly paid when due.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance only the portion of capital that would otherwise be kept idle
rubrics_metrics.description: What a bank can with propriety advance to a merchant or undertaker of any kind, is not either the whole capital with which he trades, or even any considerable part of that capital; but that part of it only which he would otherwise be obliged to keep by him unemployed and in ready money, for answering occasional demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If bank advances never exceed this value, paper will not exceed the coin that would circulate without paper. Banks should avoid financing the bulk of a trader's circulating capital or any substantial part of fixed capital because of mismatch in timing of returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require frequent and regular repayments from customers
rubrics_metrics.description: The banking companies of Scotland ... were for a long time very careful to require frequent and regular repayments from all their customers, and did not care to deal with any person ... who did not make, what they called, frequent and regular operations with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent repayments let banks judge the debtor's thriving or declining circumstances from their books, and they also show whether advances have exceeded the amount the customer would otherwise have kept idle. This practice reduces extraordinary expenses of replenishing coffers and helps prevent issuing more paper than circulation can absorb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor that repayments over short periods match advances; cease dealing if they don't
rubrics_metrics.description: The bank ... ought to observe with great attention, whether, in the course of some short period (of four, five, six, or eight months, for example), the sum of the repayments which it commonly receives from them, is, or is not, fully equal to that of the advances which it commonly makes to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If repayments commonly equal advances within such short periods, the bank may safely continue dealing with such customers because inflows match outflows. If repayments commonly fall very much short, the stream out of coffers exceeds that in and, unless replenished by large expense, coffers will soon be exhausted; the bank should not continue to deal with such customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not lend for fixed capital or long-term undertakings; use bonds/mortgages or private lenders
rubrics_metrics.description: Still less could a bank afford to advance him any considerable part of his fixed capital ... The returns of the fixed capital are, in almost all cases, much slower than those of the circulating capital ... the money which is borrowed ... ought not to be borrowed of a bank, but ought to be borrowed upon bond or mortgage, of such private people ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banks are suited to short-term advances matching the turnover of circulating capital. Fixed-capital projects (mines, forges, land improvements) have slow returns and should be financed by long-term creditors willing to live on interest, or by instruments (bonds/mortgages) that impose repayment discipline and protect lenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject customers whose pattern of repayments indicates over-trading
rubrics_metrics.description: If, on the contrary, the sum of the repayments from certain other customers, falls commonly very much short of the advances which it makes to them, it cannot with any safety continue to deal with such customers ... The stream which ... was continually running out from its coffers, is necessarily much larger than that which is continually running in ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customers who require continual advances without matching repayments are effectively over-trading and force banks into expensive replenishment or risky practices (drawing bills, etc.). Banks should avoid dealing with such customers or insist on different financing (mortgages/bonds) and stricter repayment terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid raising money by circulation (drawing-and-redrawing) — it's fictitious and ruinous
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of drawing and redrawing ... A in Edinburgh draws a bill upon B in London ... B redraws upon A ... this practice ... has sometimes gone on for several months, even years ... the bill always returning upon A ... with the accumulated interest and commission ... This practice was called raising money by circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith characterizes payments effected by successive redrafts as essentially fictitious: the value advanced by the first bill is never really returned to banks because a new bill is always drawn to pay the old. The method is extremely costly (commissions and compound interest can exceed ordinary profits), can sustain projects only temporarily, and often results in ruin when reality catches up. Variants described include chains of bills through multiple London correspondents and transfers by sight-bills; all are expensive and increase paper beyond what circulation can absorb.
